cards.name: Shopify product/page SEO title and meta description
cards.summary: The two fields behind Shopify's 'Search engine listing preview': a page title (field cap 70 characters, Shopify advises keeping it to 60) and a meta description (160 recommended). A good pair puts the target keyword in the first words of a title that is fully visible in the result, and a natural-sentence description that earns the click.
use_for: Product, collection, page and homepage SEO titles and descriptions for a D2C Shopify store.
Rewriting the defaults a theme generates (shop name plus content title) into keyword-first titles.
Batch SEO rewrites of a catalogue where every product needs a unique title and description.
avoid: Writing to the 70-character cap: Shopify itself says to stay at 60 to avoid shortened titles. Treat 60 as the real limit.
Leaving the fields blank: the theme then builds the title from the shop name plus the content title, which spends the visible characters on the brand instead of the keyword. Write the title.
Keyword lists ('oil, mustard oil, cold pressed oil, buy oil'): Shopify's own advice is readable, natural phrases. Write one sentence a buyer would read.
The same description on every product in a collection. Each page needs its own, with the product-specific fact (size, material, region) in it.
Assuming the 160 is a hard rule and Google will show it: it is a recommendation, and Google truncates by display width, not by count (see plat:google_search_result).

sources.title: Adding keywords to improve SEO - Shopify Help Center
sources.supports: 70-character title cap, 60 advised, 160-character description recommendation, truncation warning, blank-field default, keyword-near-the-start advice (re-read 2026-10-05)

limits.quote: You can enter up to 70 characters in the title. ... consider keeping your title up to 60 characters.
It's recommended that 160 characters is used in the description.
limits.confidence: high (Shopify Help Center; recommendation, not a field cap)

formatting: Both fields live in the 'Search engine listing preview' section ('Edit website SEO') of a product, collection or page; the homepage's are under Online Store > Preferences (Shopify Help, re-read 2026-10-05).
Text beyond the limit is accepted but 'shortened in search engine results' (Shopify Help): going over costs you visibly, it does not block saving.

The help page describes no markup, line breaks, links or emoji for these fields. Treat both as one line of plain text [inference from the page's silence, not a stated rule: save a test product and read the live result].
Devanagari titles are not addressed on the help page; if a client wants a Hindi title, test the live listing and count by what the result shows.
writing_notes: Where the hook lands: only about the first 60 characters of the title are safe (70 is the field cap, 60 is Shopify's advice). Put the primary keyword and the product type in the first words, the brand last. Shopify says 'near the beginning of the title'. Example (54 chars): "Kachhi Ghani Mustard Oil 1L | Cold Pressed | Sarson Co".

Description: one or two natural sentences, 160 characters, with the keyword once, one specific fact (volume, material, origin) and one reason to click (price band, delivery, return window) that is true. Example (127 chars): "Cold pressed kachhi ghani mustard oil in a 1 L glass bottle, pressed in small batches in Bharatpur. Free shipping above Rs 499."

Which number to trust: title 70 is the field cap; 60 is Shopify's own advice for not being shortened, so write to 60. Description 160 is 'recommended', not a cap, so the same rule applies: land the point inside 160.

Lint: `pcw.py check --platform plat:shopify_seo_fields --field title` tests the title against 70 and prints the first 60 characters as the visible text (without --field nothing is enforced). Run `--field description` for the 160. Both are counted in characters including spaces.
If the theme appends or prepends the shop name, it can eat into the visible title: after saving, read the rendered title and cut your own words to make room.
A Hinglish store title is a judgment call: check what the client's buyers actually search for before writing one, and keep Hinglish for on-page copy and social captions by default.

algorithm_notes.note: Shopify's own SEO advice: include the most important target keywords near the beginning of the title, and use readable, natural phrases and sentences in the description rather than lists of keywords.

cards.name: SMS length and encoding (GSM-7 vs UCS-2)
cards.summary: How many characters one SMS holds and how longer texts split into billed segments: 160 in GSM-7 or 70 in UCS-2 for a single message, 153 or 67 per segment once it concatenates. One non-GSM character (an emoji, Devanagari, a curly quote) switches the whole message to UCS-2.
use_for: Sizing an SMS before it is sent or registered, so it fits one segment instead of two or three.
Choosing between Roman-script Hinglish and Devanagari for a bulk campaign, with the segment cost in front of you.
Budgeting a bulk send: segments, not messages, are billed.
avoid: Pasting copy from a word processor or Google Docs: a curly (smart) quote is not in GSM-7 and flips the whole message to UCS-2, cutting 160 to 70. Retype the quotes as straight ones.

An emoji in an SMS: it forces UCS-2 for the entire text. If the client wants emoji, move that message to a channel that supports them (Twilio points to RCS for this; see plat:rcs_business_messaging) or WhatsApp.
Devanagari for a long message without showing the client the cost: the same sentence needs far more segments than in Roman Hinglish. Offer both and the segment count.
Treating the 1,600-character figure as a target: it is Twilio's API acceptance limit for the body, not a handset or carrier length, and not a good message.

formatting: SMS carries plain text only: no bold, italics or line styling. [General platform knowledge, not read on a page: verify with your gateway before relying on line breaks or tappable links.]

The encoding is chosen for the whole message from its worst character: GSM-7 (128 characters, not the same set as ASCII) if every character is in it, otherwise UCS-2 (Twilio glossary, re-read 2026-10-05).
Curly quotation marks are not in GSM-7; Twilio's Smart Encoding can swap them for straight quotes, but a copywriter should not rely on the gateway to do it.
Emoji and any Devanagari character force UCS-2. Roman-script Hinglish stays GSM-7 as long as every character is in the GSM-7 set.
Some symbols may cost two characters even inside GSM-7 (an 'extension table'); the standard (3GPP TS 23.038) was not read, so use your gateway's segment counter for any text with symbols.
writing_notes: Budget (arithmetic from the per-segment numbers): GSM-7 holds 160 in one segment, 306 in two (2 x 153), 459 in three. UCS-2 holds 70 in one, 134 in two (2 x 67), 201 in three. Each segment is billed.
India rule of thumb: 150 characters of Roman Hinglish fit one GSM-7 segment; 150 characters of Devanagari take 150/67, about 3 segments. For Hindi bulk SMS, write shorter, not the same length.

Lint: `pcw.py check draft.txt --platform plat:sms_encoding_segments --field SMS` works out the encoding (GSM-7, or UCS-2 when any character such as ₹, a curly quote, an emoji or Devanagari is outside it), counts septets (^ { } [ ] ~ | \ € cost 2) or UTF-16 units, fails a message that does not fit one SMS of that encoding (160 or 70) and reports the segment count. Without --field nothing is enforced.

Write the SMS in this order: the action or offer first, brand and detail after. The sender header already identifies you (see plat:sms_india_dlt), so spend the opening words on what the reader should do.

Medium confidence: the segment numbers come from Twilio's carrier-gateway documentation, not from the 3GPP standard. Before a large send, run one test text and read the segment count your gateway reports.
Example that fits one GSM-7 segment (Hinglish, 101 chars): "Aapka order SC2231 aaj ship hoga. Track karein: sarsonco.in/t/SC2231. Madad ke liye reply karein YES." (Fictional brand.)

cards.name: India commercial SMS on DLT (TRAI TCCCPR)
cards.summary: In India a commercial SMS must go out under a DLT-registered sender header with content that matches a registered template. Write the template, not the message: fixed text plus a few tagged variables (three normally, 30 characters each), at least 30% fixed content, the right header suffix (-P, -S, -T, -G) and an opt-out in promotional messages.
use_for: Drafting the template text a brand registers on DLT before its first bulk or alert SMS.
Deciding which fields become variables (name, order id, amount, link) and which stay fixed.
Choosing promotional vs service vs transactional by what the message actually contains.
Reviewing a template for the 30%-fixed, 3-variable and whitelisted-link rules before it is submitted.
avoid: Adding an offer line to a service or transactional template: promotional content mixed in makes the WHOLE message promotional (TRAI 2025 text, as read in the harvest). Keep the offer in its own promotional template.
Turning every changing detail into a variable: at least 30% of the template characters must be fixed content. Keep the sentence fixed and vary only name, id, amount, link.
A link, APK, OTT link or call-back number that the sender has not whitelisted: such messages pass scrubbing only if whitelisted.

Quoting the 6-character header as a TRAI rule: the regulation speaks of an 11-character alphanumeric string; 6 characters (6 letters for service/transactional, 6 digits for promotional) is operator-portal practice reported by SMS vendors (low confidence).
A promotional template with no opt-out in the same message.
Putting Devanagari or emoji in a template without checking the segment cost (see plat:sms_encoding_segments).

limits.confidence: high (TRAI TCCCPR (Second Amendment) Regulations, 12 Feb 2025, gazette text)

formatting: Plain text with variable slots: the registered template is fixed text plus tagged variables, and the sent message is the template with the variables filled. Placeholder syntax in vendor portals is usually {#var#} [vendor convention, not read in the TRAI text: confirm in your operator portal].
Header: an alphanumeric string up to 11 characters per the TRAI text; the message type shows as a suffix: -P promotional, -S service, -T transactional, -G government.
Each variable is pre-tagged for its purpose; one template cannot be linked to more than one header.
URLs, APKs, OTT links and call-back numbers inside the message pass scrubbing only if whitelisted by the sender in advance.
A promotional message must carry an opt-out mechanism in the same message; the exact wording is set at registration and was not read.
Encoding: Roman Hinglish can stay GSM-7 (160 per segment); Devanagari or emoji switch to UCS-2 (70 per segment). See plat:sms_encoding_segments.
writing_notes: Order of work: (1) decide the message type from the content (any promotion in it = promotional); (2) write the fixed sentence; (3) choose at most three variables; (4) check the fixed share; (5) check the worst-case length against one segment.

Variable limit: 30 characters each; where content cannot fit in 30, the regulation allows more than one contiguous variable of the same type. More than three variables per template only on a justified request, so design for three.

Fixed-content test: TRAI requires a minimum of 30% fixed characters. Count the variable slots at their 30-character maximum to stay safe (conservative practice, the counting method is not stated in the text read).

Worst-case length (arithmetic): three variables at 30 characters take 90, leaving 70 characters of fixed text inside a 160-character segment. Example template: "Hi {#var#}, your Sarson Co order {#var#} ships today. Track it here: {#var#}": about 55 fixed characters against 90 at worst, so roughly 38% fixed and well inside 160. (Fictional brand.)

Lint: `pcw.py check --platform plat:sms_india_dlt --field "message body"` tests the body against one SMS: 160 GSM-7 septets, or 70 UTF-16 units when any character (₹, a curly quote, an emoji, Devanagari) forces UCS-2 (without --field nothing is enforced). Run `--field variable` (matches the 30-character row) for the 30 (put only one variable value in the file) and `--field header` for the 11. Test the FILLED message against the 160, not just the template; the 3-variable count must be checked by hand.

Header length conflict: TRAI text = 11-character alphanumeric; operator portals and vendors = 6 characters (low confidence). When naming a header in a brief, give the brand's 6-character version and say the portal has the final word.
Hinglish in Roman script is the norm for Indian consumer SMS and keeps the single-segment budget; offer a Devanagari version only with its segment cost.

cards.name: Substack post (web + email newsletter)
cards.summary: A Substack post publishes to the web and is emailed to subscribers from the same text. The save limit is 1,000,000 characters (no word limit), but the practical ceiling is email size: Gmail clips emails over about 102 KB, and links, images and the publication's header and footer all count toward it.
use_for: Writing a creator, expert or publisher newsletter issue that must read well on the web and in Gmail.
Deciding how long an issue can be before the email clips and the ending (CTA, paid upgrade) is cut off.
Turning a long piece into a series when it would clip.
avoid: Reading the 1,000,000-character figure as a length target: the real cap is Gmail clipping at about 102 KB. Plain prose is cheap; link-heavy and image-heavy issues clip first.
Putting the paid-upgrade ask, the key link or the sign-off at the very bottom of a long issue: if the email clips, the reader never sees it. Put the one essential action early.
Many images and embedded links in an already long post: both count toward the email size. Cut links to the ones that earn a click.
Writing subject-line or preview rules here: those belong to plat:email_subject_line. This card is about the post body.

sources.title: Substack Support: Why does it say Your post may be truncated
sources.supports: 1,000,000-character save limit, no word limit, Gmail clips emails over about 102 KB, truncation warning in the editor

limits.quote: There's no word limit but posts over 1,000,000 characters can't be saved.

formatting: One body is published twice: on the post's web page and as the email. Both must read well; the email is the one that can be clipped.
Links, images and the publication's header and footer text all count toward the email size (Substack Support); a long post shows a truncation warning in the editor.

The Substack support page read does not list which text styles, embeds or footnotes the editor supports: [unverified here; check in the editor] and use the editor's own toolbar rather than Markdown assumptions.

Devanagari is plain UTF-8 text and is not mentioned on the page. Inference, not a stated rule: Devanagari takes about 3 bytes per character in UTF-8, so a Hindi issue may approach the 102 KB mark at fewer characters than a Roman-script one. Test a long Hindi issue by sending it to a Gmail test account.
Substack lets you A/B test titles (support article 36026518014100); subject-line craft is covered by plat:email_subject_line.
writing_notes: Lint: the FIRST (only) limit is 1,000,000 characters, so `pcw.py check --platform plat:substack_post` will essentially never fail. Judge length with the genre card's word range and by sending a test email, not by this number.

Order the issue for the clip: opening hook and the one thing the issue delivers first; the main link or CTA in the top third; the long reference material and extra links last, where a clip costs least.
Count what you add: every link, image and embedded card spends email size. A 1,800-word essay with three links and one image is safer than the same words with 25 links.
Series rule: if an issue needs to be long, split it into parts with a 'next issue' line instead of pushing past the clipping point.
For Hindi or Hinglish newsletters, keep issues shorter than the English benchmark you would use, and test one real issue in Gmail before committing the client to a length.

cards.name: Telegram Ads (sponsored messages in channels)
cards.summary: A Telegram Ad Platform sponsored message is a text of at most 160 characters (spaces included) with one button, shown in large public channels and bots. Good copy is one plain, specific idea with a clear action, no line breaks or lists, no gimmicks, and at most one link in the text.
use_for: Promoting a Telegram channel or bot (links in the text must point to one) to subscribers of large channels.
Writing 160-character ad text variants to test against the same button.
Reviewing an ad against Telegram's editorial rules before it is submitted.
avoid: Line breaks, bullet points and numbered lists: the guidelines disallow them, so the ad must be one flowing line. Use punctuation to separate ideas.
'CaPiTaLiZaTiOn', highlighting and gimmicky symbols or emoji: disallowed as excessive or gimmicky. Use sentence case and at most a plain emoji only if it is natural.
Vague or repetitive copy ('Best channel ever, join now, join now'): the editorial rules reject it. Say what the channel gives, how often, and for whom.
An in-text link in another format: it must be written @link or t.me/link, point at a Telegram channel or bot, and go to the same place as the ad's own link.
Using organic channel-post habits (long text, formatting): those belong to plat:telegram_message.

sources.title: Telegram Ad Platform guidelines (ads.telegram.org)
sources.supports: 160-character text including spaces, one optional link in the text, no line breaks/lists, no gimmicky caps or emoji (page re-read 2026-10-20 at ads.telegram.org/guidelines; the old promote.telegram.org address no longer answers)

limits.quote: The maximum length of the ad text is 160 characters including spaces.
ads may also include one optional link in the ad text itself

formatting: Text only: an ad is the text plus a button that opens a link (Telegram Ad Platform guidelines).
No line breaks, bullet points or numbered lists; no excessive or gimmicky caps, highlighting, spacing or symbols; no intrusive or gimmicky emoji.
One optional link inside the text itself, in the @link or t.me/link form, leading to the same destination as the ad link and (per the guidelines) to a Telegram channel or bot.
The 160 counts spaces. How Telegram counts Devanagari or emoji is not stated in the guidelines read: test a Hindi ad in the platform's editor.
writing_notes: Where the hook lands: the whole text is shown, but 160 characters is two short sentences. Sentence one = what the reader gets and the format; sentence two = who it is for or how often, plus the action that matches the button.

Lint: `pcw.py check --platform plat:telegram_ads` tests the 160-character text and counts its links against the extra-link row. The in-text link counts as characters in the 160. Buttons are not text: count them by hand.
Make the action match the button: if the button says Join, do not write 'Subscribe now' as well.
Example (137 chars, Hinglish): "Roz subah 3 line mein GST circular ka saar. Koi spam nahi, koi forward nahi. Free channel 'CA Notes Daily' join karein: t.me/canotesdaily" (fictional channel).
Test variants by changing one thing: the benefit sentence, or the audience qualifier. Keep punctuation plain; clever formatting is what gets an ad rejected.
For India campaigns, write the Roman Hinglish version first (the way the audience chats) and a Devanagari version second; count both against 160.

cards.name: Telegram profile bio
cards.summary: The 'about' text on a Telegram profile: 70 characters for ordinary accounts, 140 for Premium (documented client-config values). The docs call it 'UTF-8 length', which Telegram's own library counts in Unicode code points, so in Hindi every vowel sign and virama counts as well as the letters you see.
use_for: A creator, advisor or brand profile bio on Telegram.
A bio that tells people who you are and why to message or join, in one line.
A Hindi or Hinglish bio where the code-point budget has to be checked.
avoid: Counting only the letters you see: the limit is code points, and a Devanagari vowel sign, virama or nukta is one more, so 55 visible Hindi characters can be 74 code points. Count code points (pcw.py check does), or test in the app.
Emoji-heavy bios: an emoji with a skin tone is 2 code points and a ZWJ family 5 or more, so a few emoji eat a real share of the 70.
Treating 70 and 140 as certain: the live values are served to each client and the docs show them as example config. Test in the app before delivering a bio that sits at the limit.
Mixing this up with channel or group descriptions: those are separate fields; no limit for them was read for this card.

writing_notes: Lint: `pcw.py check --platform plat:telegram_bio` tests both bio rows at once, so in effect the non-Premium 70, counted in code points. Use `--field 'bio (Premium)'` to test 140 alone (a bare `--field bio` or `--field Premium` matches both rows and asks you to name one).
Formula for 70 characters: what you do + for whom + the action. Example (60 characters): "GST notices in simple Hindi | CA, Jaipur | DM to book a call". (Fictional.)

Hindi option: a Devanagari bio is counted in code points, so vowel signs and viramas use up the 70 faster than the letters you see. Example (28 code points, 22 visible characters): "जयपुर CA | GST आसान भाषा में". Test it in the app.
Spend the characters on nouns and the offer; drop 'passionate', 'helping', 'welcome to'.

If the client is Premium the extra 70 characters are worth one proof point (a number of clients or years), but write the 70-character version first so it works for non-Premium viewers of the profile too.

cards.name: Telegram media caption
cards.summary: The caption under a photo, video, document or audio file on Telegram: 1,024 characters (4,096 if the posting account is Premium), counted after formatting is parsed, and 200 for a story caption. Good copy is a one-line headline, two or three short lines, and one link.
use_for: Captions for image posts and promo creatives on a Telegram channel (offers, news cards, quote cards).
Deciding when a caption is too long and the post should be a text message with a link preview instead.
Story captions at 200 characters.
avoid: Writing to 4,096 for a client who is not Premium: write to 1,024. The 4,096 applies only to a Premium posting account.
A long article crammed under a picture: the better format is a text message with a link preview (4,096), per the item note. See plat:telegram_message.
Counting the formatting markup: the limit is counted after entity parsing, so bold or link markup does not count. Count the visible text.
Using the same copy for the story caption: a story caption is 200 characters (2,048 Premium); cut it down.

cards.name: Telegram text message (chat or channel post)

Long-form text that would be too long for a media caption (send as a message with a link preview).
Poll questions for a channel or group.

Counting formatting markup: the count is after entity parsing, so markup characters are free; count visible text.
Using entities for decoration: a channel post that is bold throughout has no emphasis. Bold one phrase per post.
Poll questions longer than 300 characters: write the question as one clear sentence.

avoid: Starting at 00:01 or leaving out the first timestamp: YouTube requires the first to be 00:00.
Fewer than three timestamps or out-of-order ones: the list must have at least three, ascending.
A chapter shorter than 10 seconds: the minimum length is 10 seconds, so merge tiny sections.
Vague titles ('Part 2', 'Next'): name what the viewer gets ('Reply ki last date').
Clickbait titles that do not match the section: viewers who jump and find something else leave.

Budgeting a Hindi description by bytes rather than characters.
avoid: Counting Hindi in characters: Devanagari is 3 bytes per character in UTF-8, so against the API's 5,000-byte limit a pure-Devanagari description tops out near 1,666 characters. Budget by bytes.
Using < or > anywhere (including '->' arrows or HTML): the API allows all UTF-8 except < and >, and Help says invalid characters are not allowed.
More than 60 hashtags: YouTube ignores EVERY hashtag on that video or playlist. Use three or fewer.
Unrelated hashtags to catch searches: misleading or unrelated hashtags may lead to removal of the video or playlist.
Assuming a link is tappable: URLs are clickable only if the channel meets YouTube's conditions (API note); do not depend on it for a key CTA.

Hashtags: choose at most three that describe the video. Put them last so they do not break the summary.

cards.name: YouTube community post
cards.summary: A text, image, poll or quiz post in a channel's Posts tab. Polls and quizzes take up to four answers; text poll options are 65 characters, image poll captions 36, quiz answers 80 (30 with an image); a post holds up to 10 images. The help page states no limit for the post text itself.
use_for: Community polls to decide the next video topic.
Quiz posts that test a viewer on the topic of a recent video.
Short channel updates with an image, between uploads.
avoid: Writing poll options as full sentences: text options are 65 characters and image captions only 36. Use noun phrases.
More than four answers: polls and quizzes allow up to four.
Image-poll captions that explain the picture: with 36 characters, name the option only.
Quiz answers over 30 characters when an image is added (80 without).
Assuming no limit means long is good: the help page states none, but Posts are read in a feed, so keep them short.

Poll formula: one question, three or four parallel options, each a noun phrase. Example (Hinglish): question "Agla video kis topic par banau?" with options "Mutual fund SIP kaise shuru karein" (34 chars) and "80C tax saving ke asaan tareeke" (31 chars).
Image-poll captions (36): the option's name only, for example "80C ke tareeke" (14 chars).
Post copy: a question or one line of news plus the action. The channel's audience sees it between videos, so reference the last upload by name.
Quiz: one question with one correct answer and two or three plausible wrong ones; keep each answer under 80 (30 with an image).

cards.name: YouTube video tags
cards.summary: The hidden keyword tags on a YouTube video: 500 characters in total, commas included, with quotation marks added (and counted) around any tag that contains a space. YouTube says tags play a minimal role in discovery, mostly to cover common misspellings, so write a short list of variants and not a keyword dump.
use_for: Adding the spelling variants viewers actually type (Roman Hinglish forms of a Hindi title, brand-name misspellings).
Filling the tags field on upload when a client expects it, within the 500-character budget.
Checking a tag list against the character limit.
avoid: Expecting tags to drive reach: YouTube Help says tags play a minimal role; the title, thumbnail and description matter more. Put the effort there.
Forgetting the counting: commas count toward the 500 and a tag containing a space is wrapped in quotation marks that also count.
Repeating the title words in 30 tags: use a few variants and misspellings instead.
Adding tags unrelated to the video to catch traffic: YouTube's own guidance is that tags mainly cover misspellings, so keep them true to the content.

What to include: the exact target phrase first, then Roman Hinglish and misspelled variants, the brand and channel name, and the language. This matches how YouTube describes tags, a help for common misspellings.
Hindi title: add the Roman form beside the Devanagari one, since viewers may search in either script.
Keep the rest of the effort for the title, the thumbnail and the description, which YouTube says matter more.

cards.name: YouTube video title
cards.summary: The title of a YouTube video, long-form or Short: up to 100 characters, any UTF-8 except < and >. No display cut-off was read, so treat 100 as a cap, not a safe length. Good titles put the topic and the promise in the first words and match what the video delivers.
use_for: Titles for long-form videos and Shorts, in English, Hindi or Hinglish.
Writing several title options to test against one thumbnail.
Checking a title for the character limit and the forbidden characters.
avoid: Using < or > (including '->' arrows or '<3'): the API rejects them.
Treating 100 as a target: no display cut-off was read, so a long title may be cut off on some screens. Keep the topic and the promise at the front.
A title that promises something the video does not deliver: viewers leave and the title works against you.
Treating Shorts as a different field: Shorts use the same title field and no separate limit was found.

Shorts use the same title field; no separate title or description limit for Shorts was found on YouTube Help on 2026-10-04.
No visible cut-off is recorded for titles; how Devanagari and emoji are counted was not read: test in Studio.

Formula: the topic or question, the specific promise, then an optional qualifier. Example (57 chars): "GST Notice Aaya? Reply Kaise Karein (Step by Step, Hindi)".
Where the hook lands: no official cut-off was read, so write as if a viewer sees about the first 50 characters [practitioner heuristic, not a platform rule] and put the keyword and the promise there.
Write three to five variants; the title and the thumbnail text share the job, so do not repeat the same words in both.
Hindi or Hinglish: choose the script the audience searches in and keep proper nouns in Roman if viewers type them that way.

cards.name: YouTube / Google video ad text
cards.summary: The text that accompanies YouTube video ads: video action campaigns (headline 30, long headline 90, description 90, call to action 10), in-feed video ads (two headline lines of 40, two description lines of 35) and Masthead (recommended 40, 60 and 15). The video carries the message; this text supports it.
use_for: Writing the headline, long headline, description and CTA set for a video action campaign.
In-feed video ad headlines and descriptions written as separate lines.
Masthead copy at the recommended lengths.
avoid: Counting one pool of characters: each format has its own fields. Write to the format you are buying.
A CTA over 10 characters for video action (15 recommended for Masthead): use a short verb ('Enrol now', 9).

Relying on the text to carry the offer: in-feed headlines are excluded from desktop and TV watch pages and may not show on mobile, and descriptions do not appear on the desktop watch page or TV. The first seconds of the video must make the offer.
Treating Masthead figures as hard maxima: Google lists them as recommended lengths.
Using organic title habits: organic YouTube titles and descriptions belong to plat:youtube_title and plat:youtube_description.

Description (78): "Live classes, filing templates and a CA doubt-clearing session. Starts Monday." CTA (9): "Enrol now". (Fictional course.)

In-feed: two headline lines of up to 40 and two description lines of up to 35, each its own sentence. Example headline (31): "GST filing, explained in 7 days"; description lines (31, 28): "Hindi course for small business" and "Live classes. Starts Monday."
Because text may not show, write the offer into the first five seconds of the video and use the text for the reinforcement: price, date, the one next step.
Keep the CTA a single verb phrase that matches the landing page (Enrol now, Book a demo).
Hinglish creative can run with a Roman headline; keep the CTA in plain English if the audience reads it that way.
